```{r setup}
#| include: false
source(here::here("R", "area_report_helpers.R"))
X    <- readRDS(here::here("data", "area_west_sussex.rds"))       # R/17_area_analysis.R
TR   <- readRDS(here::here("data", "trust_effects.rds"))          # R/19_trust_effects.R
DE   <- readRDS(here::here("data", "district_effects.rds"))       # R/18_district_effects.R
LADS <- readRDS(here::here("data", "sussex_lads.rds"))            # R/19b_sussex_boundaries.R
FOCUS <- "West Sussex"; ES_ <- "East Sussex"; BH <- "Brighton and Hove"
AREAS <- c(FOCUS, ES_, BH)

S   <- X$schools
NAT <- X$national
latest <- X$latest_panel
abs_last <- tail(X$abs_years, 1)
GOV <- gov_table(X, TR, DE)

prof <- X$profiles |> filter(year_label == latest)
p_at <- function(la) prof |> filter(LANAME == la)
p_ws <- p_at(FOCUS); p_es <- p_at(ES_); p_bh <- p_at(BH)
n_las <- p_ws$n_las

eff <- X$effects
e_at <- function(la, g) eff |> filter(la == !!la, group == g)
r27 <- function(out, la, spec) X$r27[[out]] |> filter(la == !!la, spec == !!spec) |> pull(rank)

ser  <- X$abs_series
s_at <- function(area, tp, col = "abs_rate") ser[[col]][ser$area == area & ser$time_period == tp]
rk   <- X$abs_ranks
rk_at <- function(la, tp, col = "rank_abs") rk[[col]][rk$la_name == la & rk$time_period == tp]
n_la_abs <- rk$n_la[rk$time_period == abs_last][1]

ctx  <- X$abs_context
c_at <- function(la) ctx |> filter(LANAME == la)

dec   <- X$decomp
d_get <- function(la, g, comp) dec$points[dec$la == la & dec$group == g & dec$component == comp]
d_tot <- function(la, g) { x <- dec |> filter(la == !!la, group == g) |> slice(1); x$la_att8 - x$nat_att8 }
place <- function(la, g) d_get(la, g, "Region") + d_get(la, g, "Local authority effect")

rs <- X$reasons |> filter(time_period == abs_last)
rs_w <- rs |> select(area, reason, pp) |> pivot_wider(names_from = area, values_from = pp)
r_at <- function(area, r) rs_w[[area]][rs_w$reason == r]
gap_tot <- s_at(FOCUS, abs_last) - s_at("England", abs_last)

ex_la <- X$excl$la; ex_last <- max(ex_la$time_period)
ex_at <- function(la, tp, col = "susp_rate") ex_la[[col]][ex_la$la_name == la & ex_la$time_period == tp]
ex_eng <- function(tp, col = "susp_rate") X$excl$england[[col]][X$excl$england$time_period == tp]

js <- X$joint$schools
js_ws <- js |> filter(URN %in% X$urns)
sc <- X$scenarios; sc_above <- sc |> filter(absence > NAT$absence)

lp <- X$lad_profiles |> filter(LANAME == FOCUS, year_label == latest)
dva <- DE$sussex_va |> filter(LANAME == FOCUS) |>
  group_by(lad) |> summarise(n = n(), va = mean(va), neg = sum(va < 0), .groups = "drop")
aov_ws <- summary(aov(va ~ lad, data = DE$sussex_va |> filter(LANAME == FOCUS)))[[1]]
fe <- function(o, s, l) DE$focus |> filter(la == FOCUS, outcome == o, spec == s, lad == l)
S0 <- "Published specification"; S1 <- "With a school term"
```

## Draft for discussion

A first draft, written as a companion to the
[East Sussex document](east_sussex.html) and to
[How to Pull the Right Lever](https://adamdennett.github.io/school_attainment_tool/pulling_the_right_lever_v2.html).
Every figure comes from published Department for Education data and the
national models documented there. Nothing uses pupil-level records.
:::

# Summary {.unnumbered}

**West Sussex's results look ordinary, but its pupils should be doing
better.** In `r latest` the county's `r nrow(S)` state-funded secondary
schools averaged `r pts(p_ws$att8)` in Attainment 8, close to England's
`r pts(NAT$att8)` (`r ord(p_ws$rank_att8)` of `r n_las` authorities). But
its schools are among the least disadvantaged in England
(`r pp(p_ws$fsm)`% against `r pp(NAT$fsm)`%, `r ord(n_las - p_ws$rank_fsm + 1)`
lowest). Its disadvantaged pupils average `r pts(p_ws$att8_dis)`, against
`r pts(NAT$att8_dis)` nationally (`r ord(p_ws$rank_att8_dis)`).

- **The county's schools get less from their pupils than the model
  expects, and this is the main finding.** Once intake and circumstances
  are accounted for, West Sussex ranks `r ord(e_at(FOCUS, "All pupils")$rank)`
  of `r e_at(FOCUS, "All pupils")$n_las` for all pupils. For disadvantaged
  pupils it ranks `r ord(e_at(FOCUS, "Disadvantaged")$rank)` of
  `r e_at(FOCUS, "Disadvantaged")$n_las`, significantly below average.
  The local authority effect costs disadvantaged pupils about
  `r pts(-d_get(FOCUS, "Disadvantaged", "Local authority effect"))`
  Attainment 8 points.
- **Absence is not the explanation here, unlike in East Sussex and
  Brighton and Hove.** The county's absence (`r pp(s_at(FOCUS, abs_last))`%
  in autumn and spring `r yr(abs_last)`) is close to England's
  (`r pp(s_at("England", abs_last))`%) and almost exactly what its intake
  predicts. Controlling for it makes no difference to the county's
  standing: `r ord(r27("dis", FOCUS, "A-raw"))` with it,
  `r ord(r27("dis", FOCUS, "A-none"))` without.
- **What absence there is has a distinctive shape.** Illness runs above
  the national rate and unauthorised absence below it. Reduced timetables
  run at `r sprintf("%.1f", r_at(FOCUS, "Reduced timetable") / r_at("England", "Reduced timetable"))`
  times the national rate, the clearest outlier in the county's absence
  profile.
- **Crawley is a real district effect.** All `r dva$n[dva$lad == "Crawley"]`
  of its schools sit below expectation. For non-disadvantaged pupils its
  effect survives even when each school's own record is taken into
  account, the only district in Sussex where it does.
- **Who runs a school matters less than which school it is.**
  `r sum(GOV$trust_kind == "Maintained")` of the county's schools are
  maintained and `r sum(GOV$trust_kind == "Multi-academy trust")` are in
  multi-academy trusts. United Learning's three West Sussex schools are
  among the county's strongest. The Kemnal Academies Trust's schools run
  significantly more absence than their intakes predict.

# About this analysis

This document applies the national models of the Lever report to West
Sussex in the same way the [East Sussex document](east_sussex.html) does
for that county. Its sections follow the same order, and its methods are
described in full there. In brief:

- **The models are the published ones:** multilevel models of
  school-level Attainment 8 for every state-funded mainstream secondary
  school in England, 2021/22 to 2024/25, for all, disadvantaged and
  non-disadvantaged pupils. They explain around 80% of the variation
  between schools.
- **Three sections refit copies of them** to ask questions the published
  versions cannot: @sec-districts adds a district level, @sec-trusts a
  multi-academy trust level, and @sec-plane separates absence from
  intake.
- **Absence runs to autumn and spring `r yr(abs_last)`**, and the
  value-added tables include provisional 2025/26 results.
- **The models describe schools, not pupils.** They show how strongly a
  school's characteristics and its results move together across England.
  They cannot show that one causes the other for any child, and the
  scenarios are indications of scale, not forecasts.

# The county's schools

```{r map}
#| fig-cap: "West Sussex's state-funded secondary schools, coloured by overall absence in 2024/25, within the county's seven districts and boroughs. Choose another measure from the menu above the map; circle size is the school's roll. Hover over a school for its figures and who runs it."
map_area(X, GOV, LADS, height = 600)
```

West Sussex has `r nrow(S)` state-funded mainstream secondary schools
teaching `r format(sum(S$pupils), big.mark = ",")` pupils, across seven
districts and boroughs:

- **Crawley**, a new town by Gatwick.
- **The market towns of Horsham and Mid Sussex.**
- **The coast**, from Selsey and Bognor Regis through Littlehampton and
  Worthing to Shoreham.
- **Chichester and its rural hinterland.**

All the schools are non-selective. `r sum(S$religion %in% c("Roman Catholic"))`
are Catholic and `r sum(grepl("Church of England", S$religion))` Church of
England. Like East Sussex, the county also has a large independent
sector, which is outside these models.

```{r districts}
#| tbl-cap: "Schools by district and borough, 2024/25. Unweighted school means."
district_table(S)
```

```{r district-notes}
#| include: false
lp_c <- lp |> filter(lad == "Crawley")
lp_rich <- lp |> filter(lad %in% c("Horsham", "Mid Sussex"))
```

The county divides sharply. Horsham and Mid Sussex are the least
disadvantaged districts in Sussex (`r pp(min(lp_rich$fsm))` to
`r pp(max(lp_rich$fsm))`% eligible for free school meals), arrive with
the highest prior attainment and average over 49 in Attainment 8.
Crawley is the most disadvantaged (`r pp(lp_c$fsm, 0)`%). It has the
lowest results (`r pts(lp_c$att8)`), and its disadvantaged pupils average
`r pts(lp_c$att8_dis)`. The coastal districts of Arun and Chichester sit
between, with results almost as low as Crawley's on a less disadvantaged
intake.

```{r school-table}
#| tbl-cap: "Every state-funded secondary school, 2024/25. KS2 is the cohort's mean Key Stage 2 score, centred as in the national model (England's school average is about 4.5)."
school_table(S)
```

## Who runs the county's schools {#sec-governance}

```{r gov-counts}
#| include: false
n_maint <- sum(GOV$trust_kind == "Maintained")
n_mat   <- sum(GOV$trust_kind == "Multi-academy trust")
n_sat   <- sum(GOV$trust_kind == "Single-academy trust")
n_spons <- sum(GOV$route == "Sponsor-led academy")
n_trusts <- n_distinct(GOV$run_by[GOV$trust_kind == "Multi-academy trust"])
chg <- GOV |> filter(changed)
```

Nearly half of West Sussex's secondary schools are still maintained. In
`r yr("202425")`:

- **`r n_maint` were maintained** by the county council.
- **`r n_mat` were in `r n_trusts` multi-academy trusts.** These range
  from national trusts (United Learning, Ormiston, Kemnal, Woodard) to
  local ones of two or three schools.
- **`r n_sat` was a single-academy trust.**

`r n_spons` academies are sponsored: placed with a trust, usually
because they were struggling. They are mostly on the coast.

```{r fig-governance}
#| fig-cap: "Who ran each school in 2024/25, and how far its results sat above or below the national model's expectation over 2021/22 to 2024/25 (Attainment 8 points). Each panel is a governing body; each dot a school, coloured by district and shaped by how it came to be run that way."
#| fig-height: 11
fig_governance(GOV, "West Sussex's schools by who ran them in 2024/25")
```

```{r tbl-gov-change}
#| tbl-cap: "Schools whose governing body has changed since 2024/25, from Get Information about Schools (October 2026)."
chg |>
  transmute(School = ifelse(!is.na(name_now) & name_now != SCHNAME,
                            paste0(SCHNAME, " → ", name_now), SCHNAME),
            District = district, `Run by, 2024/25` = run_by, `Run by now` = run_by_now) |>
  kt(align = "llll")
```

Governance shows no simple pattern. The strongest school on value added,
St Oscar Romero in Worthing, is maintained. So are several of the
weakest, including St Wilfrid's in Crawley. United Learning's three
sponsored academies are all above expectation. @sec-trusts asks the
question formally.

# How West Sussex compares

```{r profile-table}
#| tbl-cap: "West Sussex, East Sussex, Brighton and Hove and England, 2024/25. Means of school-level figures; ranks among all local authorities (1 = highest)."
row <- function(lab, col, d = 1) {
  f <- function(x) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), x)
  rnk <- function(p) sprintf("%s (%s)", f(p[[col]]), ord(rank(-prof[[col]])[prof$LANAME == p$LANAME]))
  tibble(Measure = lab, `West Sussex` = rnk(p_ws), `East Sussex` = rnk(p_es),
         `Brighton and Hove` = rnk(p_bh),
         England = f(sum(prof[[col]] * prof$schools, na.rm = TRUE) /
                       sum(prof$schools[!is.na(prof[[col]])])))
}
bind_rows(
  row("Attainment 8, all pupils", "att8"),
  row("Attainment 8, disadvantaged", "att8_dis"),
  row("Attainment 8, non-disadvantaged", "att8_non"),
  row("Disadvantage gap (points)", "gap"),
  row("Disadvantaged (FSM6) %", "fsm"),
  row("Overall absence %", "absence"),
  row("Persistent absence %", "persistent"),
  row("Mean KS2 (centred)", "ks2_c", 2),
  row("EAL %", "eal"),
  row("EHC plan %", "sen_ehcp")) |>
  kt(align = "lrrrr")
```

Against England, West Sussex has:

- **average results** overall, but a wide disadvantage gap
  (`r pts(p_ws$gap)` points, `r ord(p_ws$rank_gap)` widest);
- **few disadvantaged pupils** (`r pp(p_ws$fsm)`%);
- **average absence** (`r pp(p_ws$absence)`% on the school-mean measure);
- **slightly lower prior attainment** than the national average, despite
  its affluence.

That combination is the puzzle. A county this advantaged would be
expected to sit well above the national average. It sits on it.

```{r trend}
#| fig-cap: "Attainment 8 for disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged pupils, school means, 2021/22 to 2024/25."
#| fig-height: 4.8
nat_y <- X$profiles |> group_by(year_label) |>
  summarise(att8_dis = weighted.mean(att8_dis, schools, na.rm = TRUE),
            att8_non = weighted.mean(att8_non, schools, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(LANAME = "England")
X$profiles |> filter(LANAME %in% AREAS) |>
  select(year_label, LANAME, att8_dis, att8_non) |> bind_rows(nat_y) |>
  pivot_longer(c(att8_dis, att8_non), names_to = "grp", values_to = "att8") |>
  mutate(grp = recode(grp, att8_dis = "Disadvantaged pupils", att8_non = "Non-disadvantaged pupils"),
         LANAME = factor(LANAME, c(AREAS, "England"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(year_label, att8, colour = LANAME, group = LANAME)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~grp, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = AREA_COL, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Attainment 8",
       title = "West Sussex's disadvantaged pupils trail England every year") +
  theme_note()
```

# What explains attainment in West Sussex {#sec-decomp}

The national model's prediction for each school adds up exactly, factor
by factor, to the gap between an area's average and England's. The
[East Sussex document](east_sussex.html#sec-decomp) explains the method.

```{r fig-decomp}
#| fig-cap: "Why average Attainment 8 differs from England's, by factor, all school-years 2021/22 to 2024/25. Approximate Attainment 8 points; the pieces sum to the total printed in each panel."
#| fig-height: 9
fig_decomp(dec, AREAS, c("All pupils", "Disadvantaged"))
```

```{r decomp-table}
#| tbl-cap: "The decomposition for West Sussex, in Attainment 8 points. Region and local authority together are 'place'."
decomp_table(dec, FOCUS)
```

**For all pupils**, West Sussex is only
`r pts(-d_tot(FOCUS, "All pupils"))` points below England, but that small
total hides large pieces pulling in opposite directions:

- **Lifting the county:**
  - its low disadvantage (+`r pts(d_get(FOCUS, "All pupils", "Disadvantage (% FSM)"), 2)`);
  - better Ofsted ratings (+`r pts(d_get(FOCUS, "All pupils", "Ofsted rating"), 2)`);
  - its teacher workforce (+`r pts(d_get(FOCUS, "All pupils", "Teacher workforce"), 2)`).
- **Pulling it down:**
  - lower prior attainment (`r pts(d_get(FOCUS, "All pupils", "Prior attainment (KS2)"), 2)`);
  - place (`r pts(place(FOCUS, "All pupils"), 2)`), of which the county's
    own effect is `r pts(d_get(FOCUS, "All pupils", "Local authority effect"), 2)`.

Absence contributes almost nothing either way
(`r sgn(d_get(FOCUS, "All pupils", "Absence"), 2)`).

**For disadvantaged pupils** the gap is
`r pts(-d_tot(FOCUS, "Disadvantaged"))` points, and almost all of it is
place: `r pts(place(FOCUS, "Disadvantaged"), 2)` points, of which
`r pts(d_get(FOCUS, "Disadvantaged", "Local authority effect"), 2)` is the
county's own effect. The rest is the South East's regional effect, which
East Sussex shares.

**This is the sharpest contrast in Sussex.**

- In **East Sussex**, the gap is absence and prior attainment, and the
  county's schools do about what is expected.
- In **Brighton and Hove**, absence costs the most, and the city's
  schools more than make up for it.
- In **West Sussex**, absence is not the issue. The county's schools get
  less than expected from pupils who are, on paper, advantaged, and
  most of all from those who are not.

# The county's own effect

```{r fig-caterpillar}
#| fig-cap: "Local authority effects from the published national models, disadvantaged pupils, every authority in England with a 95% interval."
#| fig-height: 5.5
fig_caterpillar(eff, AREAS, "Disadvantaged",
                "West Sussex sits in the bottom sixth for its disadvantaged pupils")
```

```{r tbl-effects}
#| tbl-cap: "Local authority effects and ranks (1 = best). 'Significant' means the 95% interval excludes zero."
eff |> filter(la %in% AREAS) |>
  transmute(Group = group, `Local authority` = la,
            `Effect (%)` = sprintf("%+.1f", pct(effect)),
            Rank = sprintf("%s of %d", ord(rank), n_las),
            Significant = ifelse(sig, "Yes", "No")) |>
  arrange(Group, `Local authority`) |>
  kt(align = "llrrl")
```

West Sussex's schools sit below expectation for every group:

- **disadvantaged pupils:**
  `r sprintf("%+.1f", pct(e_at(FOCUS, "Disadvantaged")$effect))`%,
  `r ord(e_at(FOCUS, "Disadvantaged")$rank)`;
- **non-disadvantaged pupils:**
  `r sprintf("%+.1f", pct(e_at(FOCUS, "Non-disadvantaged")$effect))`%,
  `r ord(e_at(FOCUS, "Non-disadvantaged")$rank)`.

Both are significant. This is a county-wide pattern across 40 schools
and four years, not one or two schools.

Unlike Brighton and Hove, the ranking does not depend on absence. With
the absence control the county is `r ord(r27("dis", FOCUS, "A-raw"))` for
disadvantaged pupils; without it, `r ord(r27("dis", FOCUS, "A-none"))`.
The county's attendance is not hiding effective schools, and it is not
what holds the schools back.

What the model cannot say is *why*. The local authority effect is
whatever the county's schools share that the model does not measure:

- how schools are supported and challenged;
- how pupil premium funding is used;
- curriculum and entry decisions;
- the recruitment market in the county;
- the expectations families and schools hold.

Identifying it would need the county's own knowledge. This document can
only point to it.

## Do the districts differ? {#sec-districts}

The district test in the [East Sussex document](east_sussex.html#sec-districts)
was run for every district in England. A district level is added to the
national model, once on the published specification and once with each
school's own record in the model too.

```{r fig-districts}
#| fig-cap: "West Sussex's seven districts: district effect on Attainment 8 (all pupils and disadvantaged) and on absence, with 95% intervals, before and after adding a school term. Effects are over and above the county's own effect."
#| fig-height: 6
fig_district_effects(DE, FOCUS, "Crawley stands out, and stays out once schools are counted")
```

On the published specification:

- **Crawley** is `r pp(-pct(fe("All pupils", S0, "Crawley")$effect))`% below
  expectation for all pupils, and significantly so.
- **Worthing** is `r pp(pct(fe("Non-disadvantaged", S0, "Worthing")$effect))`%
  above for non-disadvantaged pupils.

A plain comparison of the county's 40 schools agrees that value added
differs by district (F = `r sprintf("%.1f", aov_ws[["F value"]][1])`,
p = `r sprintf("%.3f", aov_ws[["Pr(>F)"]][1])`).

**Crawley is different from Hastings.** In East Sussex, Hastings' effect
disappeared once each school's own record was in the model, because it
was two schools. In Crawley:

- **every school is below expectation.** All
  `r dva$n[dva$lad == "Crawley"]` have negative value added over the four
  years, from `r pts(max(DE$sussex_va$va[DE$sussex_va$lad %in% "Crawley"]))`
  to `r pts(min(DE$sussex_va$va[DE$sussex_va$lad %in% "Crawley"]))` points.
- **for non-disadvantaged pupils the district effect survives** the
  school term
  (`r sprintf("%+.1f", pct(fe("Non-disadvantaged", S1, "Crawley")$effect))`%),
  the only district in Sussex where any effect does.

The Crawley schools are of every kind:

- maintained community schools;
- a Church of England and a Catholic school;
- a converter academy in a national trust;
- a single-academy trust;
- a free school.

What they share is the town. That is the closest thing in this analysis
to a genuine place effect, and it is worth the county's attention.

```{r fig-school-effects}
#| fig-cap: "Each West Sussex school's own persistent effect from the model with a school term, coloured by district: Attainment 8 (all pupils) and absence beyond what its intake predicts."
#| fig-height: 8.5
fig_school_effects(DE, X$urns, "Crawley's schools cluster at the bottom")
```

## Do trusts make a difference? {#sec-trusts}

```{r trust-setup}
#| include: false
TE <- TR$trusts |> mutate(name = tidy_trust(trust_group)) |>
  filter(name %in% unique(GOV$run_by[GOV$trust_kind == "Multi-academy trust"]))
te <- function(n, o) TE |> filter(name == n, outcome == o)
tsd <- function(o, l) TR$vcs |> filter(outcome == o, level == l) |> pull(sd)
```

The trust test is described fully in the
[East Sussex document](east_sussex.html#sec-trusts). Nationally,
schools in the same multi-academy trust share an effect of about
`r pp(100 * tsd("All pupils", "trust_group"))`% on Attainment 8, about
the same as the local authority. It rises to
`r pp(100 * tsd("Disadvantaged", "trust_group"))`% for disadvantaged
pupils and `r pp(100 * tsd("Absence (stage 1)", "trust_group"))`% for
absence. The test allows for the route each school took (sponsored,
converter or maintained), because trusts are often given schools that
were already struggling.

```{r fig-trusts}
#| fig-cap: "The national effect of each trust that ran a West Sussex school in 2024/25, with 95% intervals, estimated across all its secondary schools in England (number in brackets)."
#| fig-height: 6
fig_trusts(TE, "United Learning stands out for results; Kemnal for absence")
```

Two of the county's trusts stand out nationally:

- **United Learning Trust** runs Midhurst Rother College, The Regis
  School and Shoreham Academy. All three are sponsored academies, and all
  three are above expectation. Nationally, its schools are
  `r sgn(pct(te("United Learning Trust", "All pupils")$effect))`% above
  what their intakes predict, and
  `r sgn(pct(te("United Learning Trust", "Disadvantaged")$effect))`% for
  disadvantaged pupils. This is evidence that sponsored schools on the
  coast can be turned around.
- **The Kemnal Academies Trust** runs Thomas Bennett Community College in
  Crawley, Chichester High School and The Academy, Selsey. Its schools
  run `r sgn(pct(te("The Kemnal Academies Trust", "Absence (stage 1)")$effect), 0)`%
  more absence than their intakes predict, significantly more than
  average. They are also
  `r sgn(pct(te("The Kemnal Academies Trust", "Non-disadvantaged")$effect))`%
  below expectation for non-disadvantaged pupils. Thomas Bennett has the
  lowest value added in the county.

The other trusts, including Bohunt, Ormiston, Woodard, Bosco and the
county's small local trusts, cannot be distinguished from average.

# Absence in West Sussex {#sec-absence}

```{r fig-abs-series}
#| fig-cap: "Overall absence in state-funded secondary schools, autumn and spring terms, 2016/17 to 2025/26. Sessions-weighted; 2019/20 was not collected."
#| fig-height: 5
fig_abs_series(ser, AREAS, "West Sussex tracks England; its neighbours run well above it")
```

```{r tbl-abs-ranks}
#| tbl-cap: "Secondary absence and persistent absence, autumn and spring terms, with rank among local authorities (1 = highest absence)."
rk |> filter(la_name == FOCUS) |>
  transmute(Year = yr(time_period),
            `West Sussex: absence / persistent` = sprintf("%.1f%% (%s) / %.1f%% (%s)",
                                                          abs_rate, ord(rank_abs), pa_rate, ord(rank_pa))) |>
  left_join(ser |> filter(area == "England") |>
              transmute(Year = yr(time_period), England = sprintf("%.1f%% / %.1f%%", abs_rate, pa_rate)),
            by = "Year") |>
  kt(align = "lrr")
```

West Sussex's absence has tracked England's closely for a decade. In
`r yr(abs_last)` it was `r pp(s_at(FOCUS, abs_last))`%
(`r ord(rk_at(FOCUS, abs_last))` of `r n_la_abs`), and the county's
absence is almost exactly what its intake predicts: `r sgn(c_at(FOCUS)$excess, 2)`
points, `r ord(c_at(FOCUS)$rank_excess)` of `r c_at(FOCUS)$n_las`.
It is not the problem that it is in East Sussex or Brighton and Hove.

```{r fig-reasons}
#| fig-cap: "Absence by register reason, autumn and spring terms, percentage of possible sessions. The ten largest reasons nationally."
#| fig-height: 5.2
fig_reasons(rs, AREAS, paste("More illness, less truancy, many more reduced timetables,", yr(abs_last)))
```

```{r tbl-reason-gap}
#| tbl-cap: "West Sussex against England, by reason, in percentage points of possible sessions."
reason_gap_table(rs, FOCUS)
```

The profile is unusual, even though the total is not. Against England:

- **Illness is higher:** `r pp(r_at(FOCUS, "Illness"), 2)` against
  `r pp(r_at("England", "Illness"), 2)`% of sessions.
- **Unauthorised absence is lower:** `r pp(r_at(FOCUS, "Unauthorised, other"), 2)`
  against `r pp(r_at("England", "Unauthorised, other"), 2)`%. The two
  roughly cancel.
- **Reduced timetables stand out:** `r pp(r_at(FOCUS, "Reduced timetable"), 2)`%
  of sessions, `r sprintf("%.1f", r_at(FOCUS, "Reduced timetable") / r_at("England", "Reduced timetable"))`
  times England's rate and the highest of the three Sussex authorities.

A reduced timetable is a decision made within the system, usually for a
pupil with additional needs while support or a placement is arranged. At
this rate it is worth the county knowing who these pupils are and how
long they stay on them.

```{r susp}
#| include: false
```

Suspensions, in contrast, are below the national rate:
`r pp(ex_at(FOCUS, ex_last))` per 100 pupils in `r yr(ex_last)`, against
`r pp(ex_eng(ex_last))` for England and `r pp(ex_at(ES_, ex_last))` for
East Sussex (`r ord(ex_at(FOCUS, ex_last, "rank_susp"))` of
`r ex_at(FOCUS, ex_last, "n_la")`).

# What absence costs, school by school

## Two signals {#sec-plane}

```{r fig-plane}
#| fig-cap: "West Sussex schools on the joint-signal plane, mean over 2021/22 to 2024/25: absence above or below what the intake predicts (horizontal) against value added with attendance counted in (vertical). Grey: every school in England."
#| fig-height: 7.5
fig_plane(js, X$urns)
```

As in East Sussex, the two signals go together across the county's
schools (correlation `r sprintf("%.2f", cor(js_ws$resid_abs_pp, js_ws$vadd_M2))`).
But the spread is mainly vertical. West Sussex's schools differ more in
what they add than in how they manage attendance. Two schools are
furthest from the centre:

- **St Oscar Romero in Worthing**, far above, with attendance well
  better than its intake predicts.
- **Thomas Bennett Community College in Crawley**, the lowest.

## What closing the gap would be worth

```{r tbl-scenario}
#| tbl-cap: "Predicted Attainment 8 gain if each school's absence fell to the national school average (2024/25), and if its disadvantage fell to the county average. Indicative only."
scenario_table(sc)
```

`r nrow(sc_above)` of the county's `r nrow(sc)` schools are above the
national average absence. The gains are smaller than in East Sussex: up
to `r pts(max(sc$gain_all))` points at The Littlehampton Academy and Holy
Trinity in Crawley, and an average of `r pts(mean(sc_above$gain_all))`
across the `r nrow(sc_above)`. Attendance still beats redistribution of
disadvantage, which buys at most `r pts(max(sc$gain_fsm))` points. But in
West Sussex neither is where the main gain lies. That is the gap between
what the county's schools achieve and what the model expects of them.

# School by school: contextual league tables

```{r va-notes}
#| include: false
vt <- va_tab(X$va, "va_ATT8SCR"); vtd <- va_tab(X$va, "va_ATT8SCR_FSM6CLA1A")
n_neg_dis <- sum(vtd$Mean < 0)
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

## All pupils

```{r va-all}
#| tbl-cap: "Value added, all pupils: observed Attainment 8 minus the national model's expectation, in points. 2025/26 is provisional."
fmt_va(vt) |> kt(align = paste0("l", strrep("r", 7)))
```

## Disadvantaged pupils

```{r va-dis}
#| tbl-cap: "Value added, disadvantaged pupils. Small groups; figures move by several points from year to year."
fmt_va(vtd) |> kt(align = paste0("l", strrep("r", 7)))
```

## Non-disadvantaged pupils

```{r va-non}
#| tbl-cap: "Value added, non-disadvantaged pupils."
fmt_va(va_tab(X$va, "va_ATT8SCR_NFSM6CLA1A")) |> kt(align = paste0("l", strrep("r", 7)))
```

:::

`r n_neg_dis` of the county's `r nrow(vtd)` schools are below expectation
for their disadvantaged pupils on average over five years. Several of
them do well overall:

- **Oathall Community College** and **Warden Park** in Mid Sussex;
- **Tanbridge House** in Horsham.

These are affluent schools whose small disadvantaged groups do markedly
less well than their other pupils, and less well than similar pupils
elsewhere. Their disadvantaged cohorts are small and the figures noisy,
but the pattern repeats across the schools. It is where the county's
weak disadvantaged effect is most visible.

# West Sussex, East Sussex and Brighton and Hove

```{r tbl-contrast}
#| tbl-cap: "The three authorities side by side. Model figures are from the national models over 2021/22 to 2024/25."
cv <- function(f) sapply(AREAS, f)
tibble::tibble(
  Measure = c("Attainment 8, all (2024/25)", "Attainment 8, disadvantaged",
              "Disadvantaged %", "Prior attainment (KS2, centred)",
              paste("Absence,", yr(abs_last), "(rank)"), "Absence above intake-predicted",
              "Reduced timetables, % of sessions", paste("Suspensions per 100,", yr(ex_last)),
              "LA effect, all pupils (rank)", "LA effect, disadvantaged (rank)",
              "Absence's cost to the gap with England (points)",
              "Place's cost to disadvantaged pupils (points)"),
  `West Sussex` = NA, `East Sussex` = NA, `Brighton and Hove` = NA) -> ct
vals <- lapply(AREAS, function(a) c(
  pts(p_at(a)$att8), pts(p_at(a)$att8_dis), pp(p_at(a)$fsm), pp(p_at(a)$ks2_c, 2),
  sprintf("%.1f%% (%s)", s_at(a, abs_last), ord(rk_at(a, abs_last))),
  sgn(c_at(a)$excess, 2), pp(r_at(a, "Reduced timetable"), 2), pp(ex_at(a, ex_last)),
  ord(e_at(a, "All pupils")$rank), ord(e_at(a, "Disadvantaged")$rank),
  pts(d_get(a, "All pupils", "Absence"), 2), pts(place(a, "Disadvantaged"), 2)))
for (i in seq_along(AREAS)) ct[[AREAS[i]]] <- vals[[i]]
kt(ct, align = "lrrr")
```

The three authorities share a region, a coastline, and a disadvantage
gap of about fifteen points. The national model sees three different
systems:

- **Brighton and Hove**: effective schools held back by an absence
  problem far beyond what its intake predicts.
- **East Sussex**: schools that do about what is expected, with pupils
  who arrive with lower prior attainment and run the absence their intake
  predicts.
- **West Sussex**: advantaged intakes, ordinary attendance, and schools
  that get less from their pupils than the model expects. This is most
  marked for disadvantaged pupils and in Crawley.

The levers differ accordingly:

- **Brighton and Hove:** attendance.
- **East Sussex:** attendance and prior attainment.
- **West Sussex:** what happens inside its schools, for its disadvantaged
  pupils and in Crawley in particular. That is a harder lever to identify
  from published data, and the most important one here.

# Implications and questions for discussion

1. **The county's own effect is the largest addressable factor.** For
   disadvantaged pupils it costs about
   `r pts(-d_get(FOCUS, "Disadvantaged", "Local authority effect"))`
   points on its own, as much as absence costs East Sussex. What do West
   Sussex's schools share that similar schools elsewhere do not?
2. **Crawley.** Every school in the town is below expectation, whoever
   runs it. A town-wide look at recruitment, intake, transport and
   provision would be a natural place to start.
3. **Disadvantaged pupils in advantaged schools.** Some of the county's
   strongest schools overall are below expectation for their
   disadvantaged pupils. How pupil premium is used in schools where
   disadvantaged pupils are few is worth asking about.
4. **Reduced timetables.** These run at nearly twice the national rate.
   Who is on them, for how long, and with what outcome?
5. **Absence is not the priority here,** and the county should not import
   its neighbours' diagnosis.
